events.title: Record number of illegal border crossing attempts forecast in Latvia

articles.text: Record number of illegal border crossing attempts forecast in Latvia Share Follow: Follow LSM on Google Photo: Aleksejs Dunda October 13, 7:12 Defence Authors: LSM English (Latvian Public Media) , Anna Luīze Ruskule (Latgales redakcijas analītiskās pētniecības žurnāliste ) The number of attempted illegal border crossings on the Latvia–Belarus border this year has exceeded the total for the whole of last year – more than 12,000 attempts have been thwarted. Border guards suggest that the 2023 record could also be broken, LSM's Latgale editorial reported on October 12. To date, the highest number of migrants prevented from crossing the border illegally was recorded in 2023 – 13,863 people. The Daugavpils Regional Directorate of the State Border Guard suggests that this record could also be broken this year. Operation Werewolf to run until end of year in Latvia October 6, 18:22 “It is highly likely, if the warm weather persists, because we know that last year, in mid-December, temperatures dropped well below freezing. That brought the situation to an end, but we still have many months and many warm days ahead of us until December. It all depends on the weather conditions and on the determination and organisation of those facilitating migrant movements – their capabilities and the number of people involved. The freezing temperatures in 2021 and 2022 did not deter people from crossing the state border illegally. Some individuals were found to have suffered frostbite. Those individuals subsequently underwent amputations of body parts,” explained Valdis Jukšs, Head of the Daugavpils Administration of the State Border Guard. Border guards are assisted not only by the authorities but also by residents. On Saturday, 10 October, in Asūne parish, Krāslava district, with the help of hunters from Konstantinova, border guards detained eight people without valid travel documents. Border guards continue to work at an increased level, and Operation ‘Vilkatis/Werewolf’ on the Belarusian border has been extended until the end of the year. Seen a mistake? events.title: Experts: French grocery store cyberattack a warning sign for Estonia

articles.text: News Iida-Mai Einmaa {{1792140720000 | amCalendar}} share Facebook X (Twitter) e-mail The dairy aisle at a Prisma supermarket in Tallinn. Photo is illustrative. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR News A cyberattack on French grocery stores Sunday that resulted in large quantities of food being destroyed is also a warning sign for Estonia, cybersecurity experts say. Hundreds of grocery stores in France were hit by a cyberattack on Sunday when hackers raised the temperature of refrigerators to as high as 50 degrees Celsius. As a result, large quantities of food were spoiled, causing financial losses for the stores. Estonia must also be prepared for a similar threat. "Things like this can happen and the threat is very real. Fortunately, Estonia has not experienced a problem like the one in France, at least to my knowledge. But that does not mean something similar could not happen at some point because of mistakes or poor cyber hygiene," said Toomas Lepik, a cybersecurity analyst at Tallinn University of Technology (TalTech). Minister of Justice and Digital Affairs Liisa Pakosta, who is attending a cybersecurity conference in Singapore, described the incident in France as shocking. She said society must adapt to the reality that cyberattacks are no longer limited to computers and information systems. At the same time, Pakosta said Estonia has some of the strictest cybersecurity requirements in the world. "We have particularly strict cybersecurity requirements for companies providing vital services, including those responsible for food security, and these requirements must be met. Companies need to ensure their software is up to date, that systems are properly connected and that they are not accessible to just anyone passing by. As for how much companies in Estonia, such as grocery stores, have done to mitigate this risk, all I can say is that larger companies responsible for food security are required to undergo audits," Pakosta said. However, these requirements do not apply to all grocery stores. Pakosta added that both the government and businesses need to invest more in cybersecurity to ensure their systems are secure. "On the one hand, we face financially motivated cyberattacks, but we also face attacks directed against our country or society as a whole. As a digital nation, we all need to pay much more attention to this," she said. Estonian supermarket chain Selver is also closely monitoring the incident in France to prevent a similar situation at its stores. It remains unclear who was behind the cyberattack in France and whether a ransom demand will follow. "I can confirm that Selver has not experienced any incidents of this kind. We are doing everything we can to ensure that it never happens. I believe every company and every retail chain has its own strict rules and systems governing how these things work. Overall, I believe we are well protected against this kind of threat," said Selver communications manager Mariann Järvela. Järvela added that the consequences of the incident in France are not significantly different from those of a power outage, a scenario for which the supermarket chain already conducts emergency preparedness exercises. -- Follow ERR News on Facebook and X and never miss an update! articles.text: 'Black Russian' sabotage group is probably a front, experts suggest Share Follow: Follow LSM on Google Photo: LSM Latgales redakcija October 12, 21:04 Defence Authors: Judīte Čunka (Latvian Television) , LSM English (Latvian Public Media) A little-known group called "Black Russians" has claimed responsibility for an incident on the Latvian-Belarusian border in early October, in which masked and armed men attempted to smuggle 20 illegal migrants into the country and later damaged infrastructure, reports Latvian Television. Analysts believe the groups may be a front for hybrid operations created by Belarusian and Russian special services. As previously reported , on the night of October 5th-6th, aggressive and armed men in masks tried to bring 20 illegal migrants from Belarus to Latvia. The escorts threatened soldiers who did not allow them to cross the border. After several hours, the masked people nevertheless entered Latvia and damaged border infrastructure. A little-known group in Belarus called "Чёрные русы" ("Black Russians"), has claimed responsibility for this incident, promising to continue similar operations. Quite why a criminal group would bother to make such a public declaration rather than remain anonymous is an open question. With face covered and voice altered, someone claiming to be called 'Neman', the supposed spokesperson of the "Black Russians" posted a minute-long video on the "Telegram" social media channel. The video says: "We officially assume responsibility for the incident on the Latvian-Belarusian border in Kaplava parish, Krāslava region. We confirm that on the night of October 5th-6th, a group of three "Black Russians" activists crossed the border and engaged in a clash with Latvian soldiers. Then they re-entered Latvian territory near the village of Matuliški, stole video surveillance cameras, damaged the equipment, and remained unnoticed." It is also stated that the "Black Russians" will continue their claimed sabotage against Belarus' neighbors. "It was just a Latvian test that they failed. Soon you will see something similar in other areas of our border. The European Union and NATO are a colossus on feet of clay that will collapse after our first strike," opined 'Neman'. Jānis Sārts, director of the NATO Strategic Communications Centre of Excellence, based in Rīga, suggests that in reality there is no such vigilante group, and that what is happening on the border is an information operation carried out by special services. Such independent groups cannot exist in Belarus and Russia, he insisted. Sarts explained that the purpose was: "To stir up this emotional aspect here, especially for those groups of people who are really worried about it... What is happening on the border is directly related to both the Belarusian and Russian authorities. What they are doing there now is a pure information operation." Sart compared it to a magician's trick, where he performs a trick with one hand and distracts with the other. Dmitry Halko, a Belarusian political refugee and military journalist living in Poland, also shares similar views. "It's some kind of special services project. How real it is physically, we don't know. But it looks like it's some kind of proxy structure, to cover up some kind of activity, to which, if necessary, some events, some sabotage on the borders, and so on, can be attributed. Namely - they're not us, they're some kind of active citizens, so to speak, expressing their position, but we're not to blame here. Well, as usual, they're the little green men, just on a new level. They were green, they became black. It's just a very convenient cover, a very convenient legend for anything. "I think the provocations will continue, we can expect an escalation, even greater than what already exists. And now they have a fig leaf to cover themselves with - it's not us, we don't know anything," said Halko. Latvia's State Security Service (VDD) has drawn attention to a group of individuals based in Belarus who call themselves "Black Russians". On October 9, the VDD initiated criminal proceedings for the creation of a criminal organization with the aim of committing particularly serious crimes against peace, as well as against Latvia and Ukraine. The VDD is currently refraining from comment, however. Seen a mistake? events.title: Estonian ex-soldier jailed in Russia after visiting his wife

articles.text: News ERR {{1792070460000 | amCalendar}} share Facebook X (Twitter) e-mail Relatives confirmed it was Artur Kirmjõe speaking in the FSB video which surfaced in June, but say his words had been put into his mouth. Source: ERR News A former Estonian Defense Forces member is currently in a Russian prison, accused by the FSB of planning to fight for Ukraine — a charge his family says was forced out of him. Artur Kirmjõe, 30, is married to a Russian national who is banned from entering Estonia, leaving him to travel to Russia to visit her. He had done so over 10 times before he was detained on April 29. In a video published by the FSB — Russia's main internal security organ — in the Vladimir oblast in June this year, a man with his face concealed states he got in touch with Ukrainian contacts and asked to join Ukraine's armed forces. "My attitude towards the war in Ukraine became sharply negative. On my own initiative, I contacted Ukrainian contacts and asked them to help me join Ukrainian military units to fight on their side against Russia," the man is heard to say. Relatives confirm it is Artur, but say he was induced to say what he does in the video. "He said what he was forced to say, but it is all lies. It is not true. He was just reading it, I don't know, from a screen or from a piece of paper," said his brother, Jüri. Artur Kirmjõe served in the EDF'Scout's Battalion. Source: ERR Artur's mother, Inga Allikas, points out the absurdity of the charges given how and why her son had traveled there. "If a person wants to go and fight on Ukraine's side, they don't take big suitcases and a cat and travel to Russia to their wife," she said. The "Pealtnägija" report was the first time Jüri and Inga have spoken publicly on the episode under their own names and faces. The family had not drawn attention to the case earlier, hoping it was a misunderstanding which would resolve itself. Now they want international attention drawn to the situation: the 30-year-old Estonian citizen faces 7 to 12 years in prison based on what they call a trumped-up confession. Artur was born in Tallinn and grew up in nearby Maardu. He is bilingual and studied in Russian for his first eight school years, and in Estonian after that. After high school he studied at the maritime academy, was conscripted, and stayed on as a regular EDF member — serving as a paramedic in the Scout's Battalion at Tapa from autumn 2018 to the end of 2020. The chain of events leading to his current plight began shortly after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. In late March that year, a couple arrived from Russia — a married couple, aged just over 20, referred to in the report as Lina and Sergei. In early April 2022 they applied for international protection in Estonia, saying life in Russia was dangerous for them due to their anti-war views. "Lina was persecuted because of her political views, which were clearly opposed to the Russian state," said her lawyer, Merili Laansoo. Indrek Aru, head of the PPA North Prefecture's border guard bureau, said not all circumstances could be commented on, but that the grounds given were checked and no sufficient basis for protection was found. Artur with his wife Liina (name changed). Source: ERR When the PPA refused protection, Sergei and Lina appealed. Tallinn Administrative Court found they were not in real danger in Russia: no criminal cases had been opened against them, they were not on any wanted lists, and the likelihood of attracting the authorities' attention was low. The pair appealed to the Supreme Court without success. In November 2023, they were banned from entering Estonia for three years — a detail that matters much in respect of what followed. "He was quite shocked. You could see he was very uncomfortable, because he started crying. Just uncontrollably," said their friend Lars-Eerik Väina. While the court cases were unfolding, a romance unfolded too, between Artur and the still-married Lina. The pair were working as security guards at the Kauplus Aasia club in Tallinn. Lina divorced Sergei in summer 2023. Since Lina had to leave Estonia a few months later, in November 2023, Artur and Lina married in Russia on June 1, 2024, at a registry office in Vladimir, 200 kilometers from Moscow. The couple said they hoped the entry ban would now be lifted, but the PPA refused again — seeing it as suspicious that the application to live in Estonia had come so soon after the marriage, which in turn had followed soon after the entry ban. As a result, Artur shuttled between Estonia and Russia more than ten times between 2023 and 2026 to see his wife. The lawyer representing them repeatedly pointed out that traveling to Russia could be dangerous, particularly as Artur was a former serviceman, but the PPA downplayed any danger. "A significant number of Estonian citizens live permanently in Russia. In this case, the specific person has traveled back and forth to Russia repeatedly. Yes, at certain stages our wording may not have been the best. I admit that in hindsight," Aru said. He added that the official information presented at the time was not meant to encourage Estonians to travel to Russia, and that it was an unfortunate choice of words. "I think those decisions are made en masse; everyone gets the same reply under their application. Nobody looks through the files, nobody looks at the applicant's background, whether it is genuinely safe for them or not," Inga said. Artur in EDF uniform with his mother, Inga Allikas. Source: ERR Inga now lives in Helsinki and works as an accountant, but she previously spent years working as a translator for the PPA. She believes official indifference cost her son his freedom. Separation from his wife has caused Artur mental health problems, the family says, and in April this year he traveled to Russia again, after six months apart. "I lived with him for about 20 years. And the fact that he went there means love told him that it was the only thing worth going for — love," said his brother Jüri. At the end of April, the FSB arrested the Estonian citizen in Lina's kitchen. Then in June the video appeared on the FSB Vladimir office's Telegram channel and spread to other outlets. In it, Artur appears to confess to anti-Russian activity. Relatives, who can only communicate with Artur by letter via Lina, believe the video statements are entirely fabricated. "Artur has never been to Ukraine, not even out of tourist interest. To comment on what the charge is based on — some correspondence that was found, maybe. I don't know," said Inga. Aru said the family's view is now seen differently in light of the arrest and detention. "But in hindsight, would that change anything? We cannot change the past. It is, unfortunately, a tragic story," he said. Lina says she is currently not facing persecution, but, citing her safety, declined to appear in the report and asked that her real name not be published.
